title: The provider
hookLine: in Persian again: He is the one who gives daily bread (Jaap)

cards: Pick up a slice of bread and count the hands. Someone plowed a field and planted the wheat, then watched the sky all summer hoping for rain.
A harvester driver, a miller, a trucker on a night highway, a baker up at four, a cashier, whoever carried the bag home. One slice, and dozens of people you'll never meet.
Behind them, the rain and the sun and the soil, which nobody made. Every meal is a long chain of giving, and Jaap Sahib names the start of it.

teach.b: In its Persian lines, Jaap says the One is rozi dihind, the giver of daily bread, and raazak, the provider.

Rozi comes from roz, a day: the day's portion, the food, the wages, the livelihood that keeps a household going until tomorrow. Punjabi still says rozi roti for earning a living, the daily bread and the daily flatbread.

Raazak is an Arabic word for the One who provides for every creature. So in the middle of all the cosmic praise, timeless, formless, sun of suns, Jaap stops at something as plain as lunch. That's very Sikh.
Guru Nanak, in Japji, says there is one Giver for all living beings, and asks never to forget that One. But notice the Sikh balance. Trusting the Provider has never meant sitting and waiting.
The three pillars Sikhs are taught are naam japna, remembering the Name; kirat karni, honest work; and vand chhakna, sharing what you have.
You earn your bread honestly, thank the Giver for it, and share it. That's why every gurdwara has a langar, a free kitchen where anyone can eat.
The bread passes through Sikh hands and goes straight back out to whoever walks in the door. In Sikh practice, the chain of giving doesn't end at your plate; it runs through it.

how: Sikhs are taught to earn honestly (kirat karni), remember the Name (naam japna) and share (vand chhakna), and every gurdwara runs a langar, a free kitchen open to everyone.

the One who gives every creature daily bread
a cook who serves food in the langar

games.q: the Provider has given your household its daily bread. in Sikh practice, what happens next?
o: keep it all; it was given to you.
share it: some goes on to others, as in the langar.
refuse it until you've earned more.
games.why: earn, thank, share: the bread passes through Sikh hands and back out again, which is why every gurdwara has a free kitchen.

practice: Hold something you're about to eat, or think of the last thing you ate, and trace it back one pair of hands at a time: who sold it, who carried it, who made it, who grew it, thanking each one silently.
Then go one step further, to the rain, the sun and the soil, and rest there with your breath. If you pray, you can thank the Giver of daily bread.

wordCard.voice: The provider. Rozi dihind, raazak: in Jaap's Persian lines, the One who gives every creature its daily bread.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: rozi, daily bread or livelihood, a Persian word; in Punjabi, rozi roti.

carryVoice: Your line: daily bread. It comes in, and some of it goes on to someone else. Until tomorrow.
